\To deploy an Antigravity agent that returns structured, predictable JSON data (which you can pipe directly into your JsonRenderer in the React frontend), you need to define your interface using Pydantic and pass it to the agent configuration.

Here are the actual objects and SDK references you need:

1. The Schema Object (pydantic.BaseModel)
Define the exact JSON structure you want your UI to receive by creating a Pydantic BaseModel.

python


import pydantic
class UiResponseSchema(pydantic.BaseModel):
    action: str
    metadata: dict[str, str]
    confidence_score: float
2. The Configuration Reference (LocalAgentConfig(response_schema=...))
When initializing your agent, pass the Pydantic class to the response_schema parameter in your LocalAgentConfig. This forces the Gemini model to strictly conform its output to your JSON interface.

python


from google.antigravity import Agent, LocalAgentConfig
config = LocalAgentConfig(
    response_schema=UiResponseSchema, # Pass your schema here
)
3. The Extraction Reference (response.structured_output())
After sending a prompt to the agent, do not rely on standard text parsing. Instead, use the structured_output() method. It will automatically parse the generated JSON and return it as a Python dictionary that safely matches your schema.

python


async with Agent(config) as agent:
    response = await agent.chat("Analyze the system status...")
    
    # Retrieves the guaranteed JSON dictionary
    json_data = await response.structured_output()
    
    # You can now send this json_data straight to your frontend over gRPC/HTTP
    # for the <JsonRenderer data={sidebarContent} /> to consume.
    print(json_data)

.slow-speed-option [type=checkbox]:checked + .slow-speed-toggle::before {
  background: var(--google-blue-600);
  opacity: 0.5;
}

.slow-speed-option [type=checkbox]:checked + .slow-speed-toggle::after {
  background: var(--google-blue-600);
  transform: translate(calc(2em - 90%), -50%);
}

.slow-speed-option [type=checkbox]:checked:disabled +
  .slow-speed-toggle::before {
  background: rgb(189,193,198);
}

.slow-speed-option [type=checkbox]:checked:disabled +
  .slow-speed-toggle::after {
  background: var(--google-gray-50);
}

@media (max-width: 420px) {
  #download-button {
    padding-bottom: 12px;
    padding-top: 12px;
  }

  .suggested-left > #control-buttons,
  .suggested-right > #control-buttons {
    float: none;
  }

  .snackbar {
    border-radius: 0;
    bottom: 0;
    left: 0;
    width: 100%;
  }
}

@media (max-height: 350px) {
  h1 {
    margin: 0 0 15px;
  }

  .icon-offline {
    margin: 0 0 10px;
  }

  .interstitial-wrapper {
    margin-top: 5%;
  }

  .nav-wrapper {
    margin-top: 30px;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 420px) and (max-width: 736px) and
       (min-height: 240px) and (max-height: 420px) and
       (orientation:landscape) {
  .interstitial-wrapper {
    margin-bottom: 100px;
  }
}

@media (max-width: 360px) and (max-height: 480px) {
  .offline .interstitial-wrapper {
    padding-top: 60px;
  }

  .offline .runner-container {
    top: 8px;
  }
}

@media (min-height: 240px) and (orientation: landscape) {
  .offline .interstitial-wrapper {
    margin-bottom: 90px;
  }

  .icon-offline {
    margin-bottom: 20px;
  }
}

@media (max-height: 320px) and (orientation: landscape) {
  .icon-offline {
    margin-bottom: 0;
  }

  .offline .runner-container {
    top: 10px;
  }
}

@media (max-width: 240px) {
  button {
    padding-inline-end: 12px;
    padding-inline-start: 12px;
  }

  .interstitial-wrapper {
    overflow: inherit;
    padding: 0 8px;
  }
}

@media (max-width: 120px) {
  button {
    width: auto;
  }
}

.arcade-mode,
.arcade-mode .runner-container,
.arcade-mode .runner-canvas {
  image-rendering: pixelated;
  max-width: 100%;
  overflow: hidden;
}

.arcade-mode #buttons,
.arcade-mode #main-content {
  opacity: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
}

.arcade-mode .interstitial-wrapper {
  height: 100vh;
  max-width: 100%;
  overflow: hidden;
}

.arcade-mode .runner-container {
  left: 0;
  margin: auto;
  right: 0;
  transform-origin: top center;
  transition: transform 250ms cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1) 400ms;
  z-index: 2;
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  .icon {
    filter: invert(1);
  }

  .offline .runner-canvas {
    filter: invert(1);
  }

  .offline.inverted {
    background-color: var(--background-color);
    filter: invert(0);
  }

  .offline.inverted body {
    background-color: #fff;
  }

  .offline.inverted .offline-runner-live-region {
    color: #fff;
  }

  #suggestions-list a {
    color: var(--link-color);
  }

  .slow-speed-option {
    background: var(--google-gray-800);
    color: var(--google-gray-100);
  }

  .slow-speed-option .slow-speed-toggle::before,
  .slow-speed-option [type=checkbox]:checked:disabled +
    .slow-speed-toggle::before {
     background: rgb(189,193,198);
  }

  .slow-speed-option [type=checkbox]:checked + .slow-speed-toggle::after,
  .slow-speed-option [type=checkbox]:checked + .slow-speed-toggle::before {
    background: var(--google-blue-300);
  }
}

#main-frame-error:not(.showing-details) #details {
  display: none;
}

@media (min-width: 240px) and (max-width: 420px) and (min-height: 401px),
       (min-height: 240px) and (max-height: 560px) and (min-width: 421px) {
  #main-frame-error.showing-details #main-content,
  #main-frame-error.showing-details .runner-container {
    display: none;
  }
}

Here's the full breakdown of the zero-trust identity pipeline, mapped to the concert analogy throughout.

The Concert Analogy
You arrive at a venue. You hand your keys to the valet (WireGuard). The valet parks your car and gives you a claim ticket (session ID). At the door, you exchange the ticket for an all-access wristband (the Ghostbridge identity sled). Every backstage door checks the wristband — not your car, not your ticket — just the wristband. Your car (the WireGuard tunnel) never enters the venue.

Stage 1 — The Valet: WireGuard Handshake & Session ID Derivation
Files: crates/op-gateway/src/wireguard_auth.rs:529-633

When a peer connects over WireGuard, the gateway derives three cryptographic artifacts:

Session ID (the claim ticket)
// wireguard_auth.rs:529-540
let input = format!("WG-SESSION-{}-{}", peer_pubkey, Self::current_timestamp());
let session_ids = self.crypto_engine.generate_session_ids_batch(&[input.as_bytes()]);
// → BLAKE2s hash → 128-bit hex string
Input: Curve25519 peer public key + current timestamp
Algorithm: SIMD-accelerated BLAKE2s
Output: 16-byte hex session ID — the peer's claim ticket
PSK (stable parking spot number)
// wireguard_auth.rs:542-593
let salt = b"WG-STABLE-PSK-2024";  // fixed — no timestamp
// Argon2 KDF over peer pubkey
Deliberately does not rotate — rotating it would lock peers out mid-session, like changing the valet lot number while cars are still parked.

Session Key (per-visit ephemeral)
// wireguard_auth.rs:595-633
let server_nonce = self.generate_server_nonce().await?;
// Argon2 + nonce → ephemeral key, rotated per connection
The Session Record (the claim stub kept by the valet)
// wireguard_auth.rs:200-215
pub struct WireGuardSession {
    pub session_id: String,        // BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp)
    pub peer_pubkey: String,
    pub psk: String,               // stable Argon2
    pub expires_at: u64,           // 1 hour TTL
    pub auth_method: String,       // "wireguard"
    pub key_rotation_count: u32,
    // ...
}
Persisted to SQLite (wireguard_sessions table) and cached in DashMap (no SQL in the hot path).

Stage 2 — The Wristband Printer: IdentitySled
Files: crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/sled.rs, crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs

Once the WireGuard session is established, a 152-byte shared-memory struct (/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat) is stamped — the all-access wristband:

IdentitySled layout (repr(C), 152 bytes):
  [ 0.. 32]  wireguard_pubkey    — who you are
  [32.. 40]  mutation_index      — which version of the schema you authenticated against
  [40.. 72]  hashed_footprint    — Blake3(current schema state) — the hologram on the wristband
  [72.. 88]  trace_id            — UUID v4 — your unique wristband serial number
  [88.. 92]  schema_version
  [92..152]  reserved
  [192..208] nextdns_profile     — e.g., "689ec7" — your VIP section access
The footprint (Blake3 hash of the live schema state) is the hologram — it proves the wristband was issued by tonight's venue, not a forgery from last week's show.

The trace_id is the serial number stamped on your wrist — immutable, linked to a Qdrant vector record for full accountability.

NextDNS Profile (the VIP section pass)
# deploy/nextdns/upsert-rewrite.py
# Profile ID: 689ec7
# Upserts DNS rewrites: dashboard.3tched.com → 10.0.0.1
The NextDNS profile ID travels with the identity sled. It tells the DNS layer which routing rules apply to this peer — their section of the venue.

Stage 3 — The Door Scanner: xray Header Injection
File: deploy/incus/privacy-xray-ingress/etc/xray/config.json:47-50

xray sits at the venue entrance. It reads the wristband (sled) and stamps the metadata onto every gRPC call:

"grpcSettings": {
  "serviceName": "Ghostbridge.StateSync",
  "multiMode": true,
  "metadata": {
    "X-Ghostbridge-Footprint": "<Blake3 footprint hex>",
    "X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID":  "<UUID v4 hex>"
  }
}
At this point, WireGuard is dropped. The tunnel delivered the peer to the door; the tunnel itself does not go backstage. xray strips the WireGuard framing and forwards a plain gRPC call carrying only the two header stamps. The car stays in the lot.

The NextDNS profile influences DNS resolution at this layer — selector_ip routing directs packets to the correct Incus container before they ever reach the gRPC endpoint.

Stage 4 — The Backstage Guard: GhostbridgeInterceptor
File: crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/interceptor.rs:34-84

Every gRPC call hits this Tonic middleware on port 18789 before any handler sees it:

pub fn ghostbridge_interceptor(mut req: Request<()>) -> Result<Request<()>, Status> {
    // 1. Wristband must be present
    let footprint_value = req.metadata().get("x-ghostbridge-footprint").cloned();
    let trace_value    = req.metadata().get("x-ghostbridge-trace-id").cloned();

    if footprint_value.is_none() || trace_value.is_none() {
        return Err(Status::unauthenticated(
            "A.N.N.A. Scribe: Missing Ghostbridge Identity Sled. Connection Dropped.",
        ));
    }

    // 2. Zero-copy mmap read of the live sled (no DB hit, no network hop)
    let (sled_ptr, _mmap) = op_identity::read_sled()?;
    let sled = unsafe { &*sled_ptr };

    // 3. Hologram check — footprint must match tonight's schema state exactly
    let expected_footprint = hex::encode(sled.hashed_footprint);
    if request_footprint != expected_footprint {
        return Err(Status::permission_denied(
            "A.N.N.A. Scribe: Temporal Hash Mismatch. Session footprint out of sync.",
        ));
    }

    // 4. Embed trace ID into gRPC extensions for downstream accountability
    req.extensions_mut().insert(trace_val);
    Ok(req)
}
Validity rule: the sled is live only if hashed_footprint != [0u8;32] AND trace_id != [0u8;16]. A zero field means the wristband was never properly stamped — instant ejection.

The check is zero-copy — the sled lives in tmpfs (/dev/shm), mmap'd directly into the process. No SQL, no network, no disk. The guard glances at your wrist under UV light in milliseconds.

Stage 5 — Backstage: gRPC Routing to op-dbus
File: crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/main.rs:94-105

Once the interceptor passes the call, it routes to the internal gRPC service:

Default: http://10.200.0.2:50051  (op-dbus, inside the privacy network)
Subnet assignments per peer come from schemas/plugin/privacy_routes.json:

{
  "wireguard_public_key": "P8c9Kjnv4B3r6C4+...",
  "assigned_ip":  "10.100.0.2/32",    // WireGuard tunnel allocation
  "selector_ip":  "10.100.0.2",       // OpenFlow packet-match label
  "container_name": "privacy-route-550e8400"
}
OpenFlow matches selector_ip and routes to the correct Incus container. The WireGuard subnet (10.100.0.0/24) exists only to give each peer a unique identity label — it is never forwarded as a WireGuard packet beyond the gateway.

A Linux user session (wg-{first12ofpubkey}) is created via loginctl enable-linger, giving the peer a D-Bus session and $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR — the backstage room with their name on the door.

Complete Flow, Annotated
[Peer]
  │  WireGuard UDP (Curve25519 handshake)
  ▼
[op-gateway / WireGuard endpoint]
  │  BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp) → session_id        ← claim ticket issued
  │  Argon2(pubkey, stable-salt) → PSK               ← stable parking spot
  │  Argon2(pubkey, nonce)       → session_key        ← tonight's coat check
  │  Write IdentitySled → /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat  ← wristband stamped
  │
  │  WireGuard framing DROPPED here ──────────────────← car stays with valet
  ▼
[xray ingress]
  │  Reads sled: footprint + trace_id + nextdns_profile
  │  Injects gRPC metadata headers:
  │    X-Ghostbridge-Footprint: <blake3-hex>
  │    X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID:  <uuid4-hex>
  │  NextDNS profile → DNS rewrites applied (VIP section routing)
  ▼
[GhostbridgeInterceptor — port 18789]
  │  Header present?    No  → 401 "Connection Dropped"
  │  Footprint matches? No  → 403 "Temporal Hash Mismatch"
  │  Zero-copy mmap sled read (tmpfs, no DB)
  │  Inject trace_id into gRPC extensions
  ▼
[op-dbus gRPC — 10.200.0.2:50051]
  │  Full access to internal services
  │  Trace ID rides every call → Qdrant vector linkage for audit
  ▼
[Incus container — privacy-route-{user_id}]
  └─ Linux user session, D-Bus activated, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR alive
Why This Is Genuinely Zero-Trust
Zero-Trust Principle	Implementation
Never trust, always verify	Every gRPC call re-validates the live sled footprint — no cached "logged in" state
Verify cryptographic state, not identity claims	Footprint is Blake3 of current schema — a stale wristband from an old schema is invalid
Least privilege	NextDNS profile scopes DNS; assigned_ip/32 scopes the subnet to exactly one peer
Full audit trail	Trace ID links every call to a Qdrant vector record — immutable, append-only
No implicit trust from network location	Being inside 10.100.0.0/24 grants nothing — the wristband check happens regardless
The WireGuard subnet is purely a cryptographic identity label — it gets the peer through the front door and into the valet system. The moment they're inside, the car (the tunnel) stays parked. Everything backstage runs on the wristband alone.

Automate deployments end-to-end with headless mode
Developers need flexibility when coding. Running Kiro CLI within the terminal is easy, you run kiro-cli and you’re in. But what happens when you want to run it remotely without you being there?

Headless mode changes that. Generate an API key, drop it in as an environment variable, and Kiro CLI runs programmatically. You can pipe inputs, script outputs, and integrate Kiro directly into your CI/CD pipelines, build scripts, or any automated workflow. Get access to every tool, every agent, every capability you’d have in an interactive session now with programmatic access. Execute prompts like generating and publishing pull requests or running troubleshooting workflows without any user input locally, enabling true automation, so you can stay focused on innovating rather than continuously monitoring your deployments. You can do this simply by changing your project structure like this:

Make keys.rs a shared module: Instead of making keys.rs a submodule of lib.rs, you can make it a shared module that both lib.rs and main.rs can access.
Modifying lib.rs: Remove the pub(crate) mod keys; declaration from lib.rs.
Modifying main.rs: Instead of using use lib::keys;, directly reference keys.rs as a module.
Here's how you can modify your files:

src/keys.rs

// Your structs and functions
src/lib.rs

mod keys;
// Rest of your library code
src/main.rs

mod keys;
// Rest of your binary code

fn main() {
    // You can use items from keys here
}
This makes the keys module a shared module between your binary and library within the same crate. This way, it's not exposed to external crates, but both your binary and library can use it.

530:     async fn update_interfaces_file(
531:         &self,
532:         bridge: &str,
533:         uplink: Option<&str>,
534:         ipv4: &Option<Ipv4Config>,
535:     ) -> Result<()> {
536:         let interfaces_path = std::path::Path::new("/etc/network/interfaces");

539:         let end_marker = format!("# END {}\n", tag);
540: 
541:         // Build the managed block
542:         let mut block = String::new();
543:         block.push_str(&begin_marker);
544:         block.push_str(&format!("# Managed by {}. Do not edit manually.\n\n", tag));
545: 
546:         // OVS Bridge with IP configuration
547:         // Use allow-ovs instead of auto to prevent ifupdown hang
548:         block.push_str(&format!("allow-ovs {}\n", bridge));
549:         block.push_str(&format!("iface {} inet ", bridge));
550: 
551:         if let Some(ref ipv4_cfg) = ipv4 {
552:             if ipv4_cfg.enabled {
553:                 if ipv4_cfg.dhcp == Some(true) {
554:                     block.push_str("dhcp\n");
555:                 } else if let Some(ref addresses) = ipv4_cfg.address {
556:                     if let Some(addr) = addresses.first() {
557:                         block.push_str("static\n");
558:                         block.push_str(&format!("    address {}\n", addr.ip));
559:                         block.push_str(&format!(
560:                             "    netmask {}\n",
561:                             Self::prefix_to_netmask(addr.prefix)
562:                         ));
563: 
564:                         if let Some(ref gateway) = ipv4_cfg.gateway {
565:                             block.push_str(&format!("    gateway {}\n", gateway));
566:                         }
567:                     } else {
568:                         block.push_str("manual\n");
569:                     }
570:                 } else {
571:                     block.push_str("manual\n");
572:                 }
573:             } else {
574:                 block.push_str("manual\n");
575:             }
576:         } else {
577:             block.push_str("manual\n");
578:         }
579: 
580:         block.push_str("    ovs_type OVSBridge\n");
581: 
582:         // Add uplink to ovs_ports if specified
583:         if let Some(uplink_iface) = uplink {
584:             block.push_str(&format!("    ovs_ports {}\n", uplink_iface));
585:         }
586:         block.push('\n');
587: 
588:         // Physical uplink (if specified)
589:         if let Some(uplink_iface) = uplink {
590:             block.push_str(&format!("allow-{} {}\n", bridge, uplink_iface));
591:             block.push_str(&format!("iface {} inet manual\n", uplink_iface));
592:             block.push_str(&format!("    ovs_bridge {}\n", bridge));
593:             block.push_str("    ovs_type OVSPort\n");
594:             block.push('\n');
595:         }

597:         block.push_str(&end_marker);

599:         // Read current file content

601:             .await
602:             .unwrap_or_else(|_| String::from("# network interfaces file\n"));
603: 
604:         // Replace or append the managed block
605:         let new_content = Self::replace_block(&content, &begin_marker, &end_marker, &block);
606: 
607:         // Write back if changed
608:         if new_content != content {
609:             tokio::fs::write(interfaces_path, new_content)
610:                 .await
611:                 .context("Failed to write /etc/network/interfaces")?;

618:     /// Convert CIDR prefix to netmask string
619:     fn prefix_to_netmask(prefix: u8) -> String {
620:         let mask: u32 = !0u32 << (32 - prefix);
621:         format!(
622:             "{}.{}.{}.{}",
623:             (mask >> 24) & 0xFF,
624:             (mask >> 16) & 0xFF,
625:             (mask >> 8) & 0xFF,
626:             mask & 0xFF
627:         )
628:     }
629: 
630:     /// Replace a marked block in text content
631:     fn replace_block(
632:         content: &str,
633:         begin_marker: &str,
634:         end_marker: &str,
635:         new_block: &str,
636:     ) -> String {
637:         if let Some(start) = content.find(begin_marker) {
638:             if let Some(end) = content[start..].find(end_marker) {
639:                 let end_idx = start + end + end_marker.len();
640:                 let mut result = String::with_capacity(content.len() + new_block.len());
641:                 result.push_str(&content[..start]);
642:                 result.push_str(new_block);
643:                 result.push_str(&content[end_idx..]);
644:                 return result;
645:             }
646:         }
647: 
648:         // Block not found, append it
649:         let mut result = String::with_capacity(content.len() + new_block.len() + 1);
650:         result.push_str(content);
651:         if !content.ends_with('\n') {
652:             result.push('\n');
653:         }
654:         result.push_str(new_block);
655:         result
656:     }
657: }

333:     /// Parse ovs-ofctl dump-flows output
334:     #[allow(dead_code)]
335:     fn parse_flows(&self, output: &str) -> Result<Vec<FlowEntry>> {
336:         let mut flows = Vec::new();
337: 
338:         for line in output.lines() {
339:             // Skip header and empty lines
340:             if line.starts_with("NXST_FLOW") || line.trim().is_empty() {
341:                 continue;
342:             }
343: 
344:             // Parse flow line
345:             // Format: cookie=0x0, duration=123s, table=0, n_packets=0, priority=100, in_port=1, actions=output:2
346:             if let Some(flow) = self.parse_flow_line(line) {
347:                 flows.push(flow);
348:             }
349:         }
350: 
351:         Ok(flows)
352:     }

354:     /// Parse a single flow line
355:     #[allow(dead_code)]
356:     fn parse_flow_line(&self, line: &str) -> Option<FlowEntry> {
357:         let mut table = 0u8;
358:         let mut priority = 0u16;
359:         let mut cookie = None;
360:         let mut match_fields = HashMap::new();
361:         let mut actions = Vec::new();
362: 
363:         let (fields_part, actions_part) = line.split_once("actions=").unwrap_or((line, ""));
364:         let fields_part = fields_part.replace("actions=", "");
365: 
366:         // Split by comma and parse fields
367:         for part in fields_part.split(',') {
368:             let part = part.trim();
369: 
370:             if let Some((key, value)) = part.split_once('=') {
371:                 match key.trim() {
372:                     "table" => table = value.parse().ok()?,
373:                     "priority" => priority = value.parse().ok()?,
374:                     "cookie" => {
375:                         cookie = Some(u64::from_str_radix(value.trim_start_matches("0x"), 16).ok()?)
376:                     }
377:                     "actions" => actions = self.parse_actions(value),
378:                     _ => {
379:                         // Match field
380:                         if !key.contains("duration")
381:                             && !key.contains("n_packets")
382:                             && !key.contains("n_bytes")
383:                             && !key.contains("n_offload")
384:                             && !key.contains("idle_age")
385:                             && !key.contains("hard_age")
386:                         {
387:                             match_fields.insert(key.to_string(), value.to_string());
388:                         }
389:                     }
390:                 }
391:             } else if !part.is_empty()
392:                 && !part.contains("duration")
393:                 && !part.contains("n_packets")
394:                 && !part.contains("n_bytes")
395:                 && !part.contains("idle_age")
396:                 && !part.contains("hard_age")
397:             {
398:                 match_fields.insert(part.to_string(), "".to_string());
399:             }
400:         }
401: 
402:         if !actions_part.is_empty() {
403:             actions = self.parse_actions(actions_part.trim());
404:         }
405: 
406:         Some(FlowEntry {
407:             table,
408:             priority,
409:             match_fields,
410:             actions,
411:             cookie,
412:             idle_timeout: 0,
413:             hard_timeout: 0,
414:         })
415:     }

417:     /// Parse actions string
418:     #[allow(dead_code)]
419:     fn parse_actions(&self, actions_str: &str) -> Vec<FlowAction> {
420:         let mut actions = Vec::new();
421: 
422:         for action in actions_str.split(',') {
423:             let action = action.trim();
424: 
425:             if action == "NORMAL" {
426:                 actions.push(FlowAction::Normal);
427:             } else if action == "drop" {
428:                 actions.push(FlowAction::Drop);
429:             } else if let Some(port) = action.strip_prefix("output:") {
430:                 actions.push(FlowAction::Output {
431:                     port: port.to_string(),
432:                 });
433:             } else if let Some(rest) = action.strip_prefix("resubmit(,") {
434:                 if let Some(table_str) = rest.strip_suffix(')') {
435:                     if let Ok(table) = table_str.parse() {
436:                         actions.push(FlowAction::Resubmit { table });
437:                     }
438:                 }
439:             }
440:         }
441: 
442:         actions
443:     }

445:     /// Convert flow to ovs-ofctl string format
446:     #[allow(dead_code)]
447:     fn flow_to_string(&self, flow: &FlowEntry) -> String {
448:         let mut parts = Vec::new();
449: 
450:         if let Some(cookie) = flow.cookie {
451:             parts.push(format!("cookie=0x{cookie:x}"));
452:         }
453: 
454:         // Table
455:         parts.push(format!("table={}", flow.table));
456: 
457:         // Priority
458:         parts.push(format!("priority={}", flow.priority));
459: 
460:         if flow.idle_timeout > 0 {
461:             parts.push(format!("idle_timeout={}", flow.idle_timeout));
462:         }
463: 
464:         if flow.hard_timeout > 0 {
465:             parts.push(format!("hard_timeout={}", flow.hard_timeout));
466:         }
467: 
468:         // Match fields
469:         for (key, value) in &flow.match_fields {
470:             if value.is_empty() {
471:                 parts.push(key.to_string());
472:             } else {
473:                 parts.push(format!("{}={}", key, value));
474:             }
475:         }
476: 
477:         // Actions
478:         let actions_str = flow
479:             .actions
480:             .iter()
481:             .map(|a| self.action_to_string(a))
482:             .collect::<Vec<_>>()
483:             .join(",");
484: 
485:         format!("{},actions={}", parts.join(","), actions_str)
486:     }

488:     /// Convert action to string
489:     #[allow(dead_code)]
490:     fn action_to_string(&self, action: &FlowAction) -> String {
491:         match action {
492:             FlowAction::Output { port } => format!("output:{}", port),
493:             FlowAction::LoadRegister { register, value } => {
494:                 format!("load:{}->NXM_NX_REG{}[]", value, register)
495:             }
496:             FlowAction::Resubmit { table } => format!("resubmit(,{})", table),
497:             FlowAction::SetField { field, value } => format!("set_field:{}={}", value, field),
498:             FlowAction::Drop => "drop".to_string(),
499:             FlowAction::Normal => "NORMAL".to_string(),
500:             FlowAction::Controller { max_len } => {
501:                 if let Some(len) = max_len {
502:                     format!("CONTROLLER:{}", len)
503:                 } else {
504:                     "CONTROLLER".to_string()
505:                 }
506:             }
507:             FlowAction::ArpResponder { mac, ip } => {
508:                 // IPv4 address to hex (e.g., 10.100.0.1 -> 0x0a640001)
509:                 let ip_hex = if let Ok(addr) = ip.parse::<std::net::Ipv4Addr>() {
510:                     format!(
511:                         "0x{:02x}{:02x}{:02x}{:02x}",
512:                         addr.octets()[0],
513:                         addr.octets()[1],
514:                         addr.octets()[2],
515:                         addr.octets()[3]
516:                     )
517:                 } else {
518:                     "0".to_string()
519:                 };
520: 
521:                 format!(
522:                     "move:NXM_OF_ETH_SRC[]->NXM_OF_ETH_DST[],mod_dl_src:{mac},load:0x0002->NXM_OF_ARP_OP[],move:NXM_NX_ARP_SHA[]->NXM_NX_ARP_THA[],load:0x{}->NXM_NX_ARP_SHA[],move:NXM_OF_ARP_SPA[]->NXM_OF_ARP_TPA[],load:{}->NXM_OF_ARP_SPA[],IN_PORT",
523:                     mac.replace(':', ""),
524:                     ip_hex
525:                 )
526:             }
527:         }
528:     }

633:     /// Generate default security flows to prevent dangerous edge packets
634:     /// These flows protect against: ARP spoofing, invalid TCP flags, malformed packets,
635:     /// packet storms, and other intrusion-like traffic
636:     #[allow(clippy::vec_init_then_push)]
637:     fn generate_security_flows(bridge_name: &str) -> Vec<FlowEntry> {
638:         let mut security_flows = Vec::new();
639: 
640:         // Table 0: Security filtering (highest priority before application flows)
641: 
642:         // 1. Drop invalid TCP flags (NULL scan, Xmas scan, FIN scan without established connection)
643:         security_flows.push(FlowEntry {
644:             table: 0,
645:             priority: 32000,
646:             match_fields: HashMap::from([
647:                 ("tcp".to_string(), "".to_string()),
648:                 ("tcp_flags".to_string(), "0x000".to_string()), // NULL scan
649:             ]),
650:             actions: vec![FlowAction::Drop],
651:             cookie: Some(0xDEAD0001),
652:             idle_timeout: 0,
653:             hard_timeout: 0,
654:         });
655: 
656:         security_flows.push(FlowEntry {
657:             table: 0,
658:             priority: 32000,
659:             match_fields: HashMap::from([
660:                 ("tcp".to_string(), "".to_string()),
661:                 ("tcp_flags".to_string(), "+fin+psh+urg".to_string()), // Xmas scan
662:             ]),
663:             actions: vec![FlowAction::Drop],
664:             cookie: Some(0xDEAD0002),
665:             idle_timeout: 0,
666:             hard_timeout: 0,
667:         });
668: 
669:         // 2. Drop fragmented packets (can be used for evasion)
670:         security_flows.push(FlowEntry {
671:             table: 0,
672:             priority: 31500,
673:             match_fields: HashMap::from([
674:                 ("ip".to_string(), "".to_string()),
675:                 ("ip_frag".to_string(), "yes".to_string()),
676:             ]),
677:             actions: vec![FlowAction::Drop],
678:             cookie: Some(0xDEAD0003),
679:             idle_timeout: 0,
680:             hard_timeout: 0,
681:         });
682: 
683:         // 3. Prevent ARP spoofing for common private networks (rate limit ARP)
684:         // Allow legitimate ARP but rate limit to prevent storms
685:         security_flows.push(FlowEntry {
686:             table: 0,
687:             priority: 31000,
688:             match_fields: HashMap::from([("arp".to_string(), "".to_string())]),
689:             actions: vec![
690:                 FlowAction::Controller { max_len: Some(128) }, // Send to controller for inspection
691:             ],
692:             cookie: Some(0xDEAD0004),
693:             idle_timeout: 0,
694:             hard_timeout: 0,
695:         });
696: 
697:         // 4. Drop IPv6 Router Advertisements from untrusted sources (prevent MITM)
698:         security_flows.push(FlowEntry {
699:             table: 0,
700:             priority: 31500,
701:             match_fields: HashMap::from([
702:                 ("icmp6".to_string(), "".to_string()),
703:                 ("icmpv6_type".to_string(), "134".to_string()), // Router Advertisement
704:             ]),
705:             actions: vec![FlowAction::Drop],
706:             cookie: Some(0xDEAD0005),
707:             idle_timeout: 0,
708:             hard_timeout: 0,
709:         });
710: 
711:         // 5. Drop DHCP packets from non-server sources (prevent rogue DHCP)
712:         // Only allow DHCP responses from legitimate servers (port 67)
713:         security_flows.push(FlowEntry {
714:             table: 0,
715:             priority: 31000,
716:             match_fields: HashMap::from([
717:                 ("udp".to_string(), "".to_string()),
718:                 ("tp_src".to_string(), "67".to_string()),
719:                 ("tp_dst".to_string(), "68".to_string()),
720:             ]),
721:             actions: vec![FlowAction::Normal], // Allow legitimate DHCP
722:             cookie: Some(0xDEAD0006),
723:             idle_timeout: 0,
724:             hard_timeout: 0,
725:         });
726: 
727:         // 6. Drop invalid source IP addresses (0.0.0.0, 127.0.0.0/8 except loopback, multicast as source)
728:         security_flows.push(FlowEntry {
729:             table: 0,
730:             priority: 32000,
731:             match_fields: HashMap::from([
732:                 ("ip".to_string(), "".to_string()),
733:                 ("nw_src".to_string(), "0.0.0.0".to_string()),
734:             ]),
735:             actions: vec![FlowAction::Drop],
736:             cookie: Some(0xDEAD0007),
737:             idle_timeout: 0,
738:             hard_timeout: 0,
739:         });
740: 
741:         security_flows.push(FlowEntry {
742:             table: 0,
743:             priority: 32000,
744:             match_fields: HashMap::from([
745:                 ("ip".to_string(), "".to_string()),
746:                 ("nw_src".to_string(), "224.0.0.0/4".to_string()), // Multicast as source
747:             ]),
748:             actions: vec![FlowAction::Drop],

765:         // 8. Prevent MAC flooding attacks - limit MAC learning rate per port

769:         // 9. Allow established connections (stateful inspection)

## User

how does creating blobs for schemna consumption affect typing for grpc-bridge converting to dbus
  objects


• It reduces how much typing the bridge has to invent, but it does not eliminate typing.

  The clean way to think about it is:

  - PluginSchema is the source
  - the blob is a sealed runtime projection of that source
  - grpc-bridge consumes the blob to create D-Bus objects and gRPC surfaces

  So the blob changes typing from “hand-authored Rust structs everywhere” to “derived contract
  artifacts everywhere.”

  Practical effect:

  - For gRPC, typing becomes stronger at the boundary because the bridge can generate descriptors and
    typed request/response shapes from the blob.

  - For D-Bus, the bridge can expose objects and methods directly from the blob without inventing
    separate schema files or ad hoc method tables.

  - For internal runtime state, the blob can carry enough structure that the bridge does not need to
    guess field meaning.

  What remains typed:

  - method names
  - argument order and field names
  - return shape
  - D-Bus object path and interface naming
  - gRPC service and method names

  What becomes less typed:

  - the bridge’s implementation code
  - the storage and transport layer between schema and runtime object
  - the plumbing that used to manually mirror schema into D-Bus and gRPC

  So the short answer is: blobs make typing more declarative and more centralized, not optional. They
  move type authority upward into the schema-derived artifact, which is exactly what you want if grpc-
  bridge is projecting D-Bus objects from schema.

Accessing tab-completion programmatically in Bash
29 Nov 2015

In working on writing unit tests for some of my utilities, I encountered a somewhat unique issue. How do you test bash-completion scripts?

Lacking an obvious answer (and wishing to avoid wading into Expect scripting), I figure my best approach would be to find a way to access the output of tab-completion programmatically.

I quickly found an answer on StackOverflow that set me on the right path. Using it as a starting point, I’ll outline a straightforward way to get the tab-completions for a particular command line. In this case I want to determine the tab-completions for git a.

First, determine the completion function used by git. To do so, run complete -p git. If you run this from a fresh terminal, you’ll likely observe the following output:

    bash: complete: git: no completion specification

This is because Bash (version 2.04 and above) loads completion scripts for most commands dynamically. That is, git’s completion script isn’t sourced until it is needed, when you enter git Tab. Luckily we can source it programmatically with the helper function _completion_loader found in /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion. So to load git’s completion script we run _completion_loader git. Be sure you only run _completion_loader for completion scripts that are sourced dynamically (it will screw things up otherwise). Once everything is loaded, run complete -p again. Note that this time the output is:

    complete -o bashdefault -o default -o nospace -F __git_wrap__git_main git

The part to pay attention to is __git_wrap__git_main, this is git’s completion function. Just in case you’re curious, __git_wrap__git_main is actually equivalent to _git, so I’ll use it as shorthand.

In case you’re not familiar with Bash completion scripts, they rely on a few environmental variables to operate. The important ones are as follows:

COMP_WORDS
    An array variable consisting of the individual words in the current command line.
COMP_CWORD
    An index into ${COMP_WORDS} of the word containing the current cursor position.
COMP_LINE
    The current command line.
    Note: While rarely accessed directly, this is used by common helper scripts (albeit indirectly).
COMP_POINT
    The index of the current cursor position relative to the beginning of the current command. If the current cursor position is at the end of the current command, the value of this variable is equal to ${#COMP_LINE}.
    Note: While rarely accessed directly, this is used by common helper scripts (albeit indirectly).
COMPREPLY
    An array variable from which Bash reads the possible completions generated by a shell function invoked by the programmable completion facility.

Bash completion scripts generally only use COMP_WORDS and COMP_CWORD to determine the current and previous words on the command lines. However there are helper functions that use some of the more obscure variables like COMP_LINE and COMP_POINT. All in all, these are used to generate a list of completions which are stored in the array COMPREPLY and then printed to the terminal. So if we want the output of tab-completion, we need to access COMPREPLY after the completion script has populated it.

Here’s a very simple implementation:

# load bash-completion helper functions
source /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion

# array of words in command line
COMP_WORDS=(git a)

# index of the word containing cursor position
COMP_CWORD=1

# command line
COMP_LINE='git a'

# index of cursor position
COMP_POINT=${#COMP_LINE}

# execute completion function
# FYI: _xfunc is a helper function for loading and calling functions from
#      dynamically loaded completion files that may not have been sourced yet
_xfunc git _git

# print completions to stdout
printf '%s\n' "${COMPREPLY[@]}"

That works alright, but what if things are more complicated? What if we want to perform programmatic tab-completion for other commands? For commands that do not load completions dynamically? For more complex command lines? What if we want to more accurately reflect real-world tab-completions?

Here is such a function:

#
# Author: Brian Beffa <brbsix@gmail.com>
# Original source: https://brbsix.github.io/2015/11/29/accessing-tab-completion-programmatically-in-bash/
# License: LGPLv3 (http://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.txt)
#

get_completions(){
    local completion COMP_CWORD COMP_LINE COMP_POINT COMP_WORDS COMPREPLY=()

    # load bash-completion if necessary
    declare -F _completion_loader &>/dev/null || {
        source /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion
    }

    COMP_LINE=$*
    COMP_POINT=${#COMP_LINE}

    eval set -- "$@"

    COMP_WORDS=("$@")

    # add '' to COMP_WORDS if the last character of the command line is a space
    [[ ${COMP_LINE[@]: -1} = ' ' ]] && COMP_WORDS+=('')

    # index of the last word
    COMP_CWORD=$(( ${#COMP_WORDS[@]} - 1 ))

    # determine completion function
    completion=$(complete -p "$1" 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $(NF-1)}')

    # run _completion_loader only if necessary
    [[ -n $completion ]] || {

        # load completion
        _completion_loader "$1"

        # detect completion
        completion=$(complete -p "$1" 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $(NF-1)}')

    }

    # ensure completion was detected
    [[ -n $completion ]] || return 1

    # execute completion function
    "$completion"

    # print completions to stdout
    printf '%s\n' "${COMPREPLY[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort
}

Fox example get_completions 'apt-get ' outputs the following:

    autoclean autoremove build-dep changelog check clean dist-upgrade download dselect-upgrade install purge remove source update upgrade

get_completions 'docker p' outputs the following:

    pause port ps pull push

get_completions 'vagrant box ' outputs the following:

    add help list outdated remove repackage update

Gemma 4 31B IT (llama.cpp)
Run Gemma 4 31B IT with llama.cpp as an OpenAI-compatible API for a wide variety of tools.

This recipe is designed to be easy for nontechnical users:

the model is already chosen for you
it downloads automatically on startup
it is tuned for a single GPU
it is optimized for long-context text chat, coding, and agent tools such as OpenClaw and OpenCode
If you want the simple version: enter a container group name, decide whether you want public or private access, deploy, and wait for startup to finish.

If you want more technical detail, read below.

The model is downloaded at startup and can take several minutes before the deployment becomes ready.
What is already configured for you:

Unsloth's unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF GGUF conversion of the Google Gemma 4 31B instruction model
the UD-Q4_K_XL GGUF file, which is a practical single-GPU choice for this model size
full 256K context length
automatic GPU layer offload
Flash Attention and fit-to-memory tuning
q8_0 key/value cache types to make long context more practical on a single GPU
public access by default, with optional Container Gateway Authentication in the form
This recipe is intentionally optimized for text chat, coding, and agent workflows. Gemma 4 is multimodal, but this recipe stays text-first by default to preserve memory headroom for the long context window on consumer hardware.

Reasoning is controlled per request. To turn reasoning on, start the system prompt with <|think|>. To leave reasoning off, do not include that token.

For technical users: if you want to change defaults, check advanced settings.

Helpful references:

Unsloth Gemma 4 31B GGUF repo

🤗 Text Generation Inference
Run popular LLMs and VLMs with 🤗 Text Generation Inference, a production-ready inference server that powers HuggingChat. Model weights are included in the container, except for custom variants.

Ensure your use is permissible under whatever license applies to the model you are using.
TGI has many configuration options that you can set as environment variables in advanced configuration, but it usually does a reasonable job of detecting the hardware and setting defaults automatically.

Supports OpenAI Messages API, streaming output, JSON mode and more.

Custom
While we have several containers with the model weights included, you can deploy TGI with any supported model using the Custom option for this recipe.

See supported models
Make sure your model fits in the vRAM limits of your GPU. This recipe uses RTX 4090 by default, which has 24GB vRAM. You can estimate the vRAM usage of a model by multiplying the number of parameters by the parameter size (2 bytes for fp16, 1 byte for fp8, etc). For example, a 7B parameter model in fp16 would use approximately 14GB of vRAM for the model weights alone, plus additional vram dependent on context length and batch size. You would want a 24GB GPU for a model of that size.
